entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: A standard first line that states the purpose of an email or letter right away.
entries.usage: Used after the greeting in neutral to formal emails, especially to people you don't know well: *I'm writing to ask about the open position*. It is followed by *to* + verb (*ask*, *confirm*, *let you know*, *follow up on*). With colleagues you write to often, you can skip it and start with the point.
entries.pattern: I'm writing to + verb (ask / confirm / let you know / follow up on …)
examples: Dear Dr. Ramos, **I'm writing to** ask whether you have space for a summer intern in your lab.
Hi Ms. Carter, **I'm writing to** let you know that Ethan will miss school on Friday.
**I'm writing to** follow up on the leak in our bathroom ceiling, which has gotten worse.

drill.sentence: Dear Mr. Patel, {{I'm writing to}} confirm our appointment on Tuesday at 10 a.m.
drill.hint: standard opener stating the purpose — three words (not *I'd like to* or *I'm emailing to*)

mistake.wrong: I am writing you because I have a question about the course.
mistake.right: I'm writing to ask about the course.
mistake.why: Style, not grammar (*writing you* is fine in American English): the *to* + verb opening states your purpose faster than *because I have a question*.

entries.related: *I'm reaching out to / because* — common in American email, a little corporate; *just a quick note to* — informal; *I'm contacting you regarding* — formal.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: A friendly request to tell you if something is true, needed or a problem.
entries.usage: One of the most common lines in American work email, often near the end: *Let me know if you have any questions*. It is neutral and works with almost anyone. Typical endings are *if you need anything else*, *if that works for you* and *if anything changes*; adding *please* makes it a little more formal.
entries.pattern: (Please) let me know if + clause
examples: **Let me know if** Thursday doesn't work for you, and we can find another time.
I've attached the updated schedule. **Let me know if** you see any mistakes.
We're ordering pizza for movie night, so **let me know if** your kids have any food allergies.

drill.sentence: Here's the revised budget for the class trip. {{Let me know if}} you have any questions.
drill.hint: friendly request to hear back in case (not *Tell me if*)

entries.related: *feel free to reach out if* — a little more formal; *please don't hesitate to contact me if* — formal, can sound stiff; *give me a shout if* — very casual.

entries.term: I look forward to hearing from you
entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: A formal closing line that says you hope for and expect a reply.
entries.usage: Standard at the end of formal emails and letters, such as job applications and first contacts, just before the sign-off. After *look forward to*, use the *-ing* form, because *to* is a preposition here. *I'm looking forward to hearing from you* is a little warmer and less formal.
entries.pattern: I look forward to + -ing / noun
examples: Thank you for considering my application. **I look forward to hearing from you**.
We **look forward to hearing from you** about a date for the next site visit.
My grandma ends every letter with "**I look forward to hearing from you**," even the ones to her grandkids.

drill.sentence: Thank you again for meeting with me on Friday. {{I look forward to hearing from you}} about next steps.
drill.hint: formal closing that expects a reply — simple present (not *I'm …-ing*)

mistake.wrong: I look forward to hear from you.
mistake.right: I look forward to hearing from you.
mistake.why: *To* in *look forward to* is a preposition, so it takes the *-ing* form.

entries.related: *I'm looking forward to hearing from you* — warmer; *I hope to hear from you soon* — simpler; *Looking forward to it!* — casual.

entries.term: thanks for getting back to me
entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: Thank you for replying to my message, usually after a question or request.
entries.usage: A very common first line when you answer someone's reply: *Thanks for getting back to me so quickly*. It is neutral and polite and works in email, text and on the phone. *Get back to someone* means reply or contact them again; the more formal version is *Thank you for your reply*.
entries.pattern: Thanks for getting back to me (so quickly / about …)
examples: Hi Dr. Lin, **thanks for getting back to me** so quickly. Tuesday at three works well.
**Thanks for getting back to me** about the apartment. Is it still available in June?
When the plumber finally called back, I said, "**Thanks for getting back to me**," and tried not to sound annoyed.

drill.sentence: {{Thanks for getting back to me}} on a Sunday! I didn't expect an answer until Monday.
drill.hint: appreciation for the reply — phrasal verb with *me* (not *for responding*)

entries.related: *thank you for your reply* — more formal; *thanks for the quick reply* — when it was fast; *I'll get back to you* — I'll reply later.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: Tells the reader that the information they need is further down in the email or in the forwarded thread.
entries.usage: Common in work email when you forward a message, answer several questions or paste details: *Please see below for the schedule*. It is neutral and efficient, but alone it can feel cold, so add a short summary or a friendly line. *See below* without *please* is shorter and a bit more casual.
entries.pattern: Please see below (for + information); please see my answers below
examples: Hi Mark, **please see below** for the parking instructions for tomorrow's visit.
Thanks for your questions. **Please see** my answers **below**, in blue.
The school forwarded the district's long message with just one line on top: "**Please see below**."

drill.sentence: Hi team, the hotel just sent the conference details. {{Please see below}} for check-in times and the shuttle schedule.
drill.hint: look further down this email — polite (not *… find …*)

entries.related: *see below* — shorter, a bit more casual; *please find below* — more common in British and international email; *see attached* — the information is in a file.

entries.label: email sign-off
entries.meaning: A polite, common sign-off at the end of an email, just before your name.
entries.usage: Safe for almost any work email, including first contacts and clients. It sits between *Best* (more casual) and *Sincerely* (more formal). Capitalize only the first word, add a comma, and put your name on the next line.
examples: Thanks again for your help with the visa letter. **Best regards**, Lena Fischer
I close emails to new clients with "**Best regards**" and just "Best" with my coworkers.
Even in a two-line email to the landlord, my father signs off with "**Best regards**."

drill.sentence: Please let me know if the new date works for you. {{Best regards}}, Daniel Wu
drill.hint: common polite two-word sign-off (not *Kind …*, *Warm …* or *… wishes*)

mistake.why: A style point: in a sign-off, only the first word is normally capitalized.

entries.related: *Best* — shorter and very common in American work email; *Kind regards* — similar, slightly warmer; *Thanks* — casual, when you have asked for something.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: Draws the reader's attention to an important detail, rule or change.
entries.usage: Common in work, school and official emails: *Please note that the office will be closed on Monday*. It is neutral to formal and fine for facts, but used about a person's mistake it can sound like a warning. *Just a heads-up* is friendlier, and *Note that* without *please* is common in instructions.
examples: **Please note that** the building will be closed on Monday for Labor Day.
All samples must be labeled by Friday; **please note that** unlabeled boxes will be thrown out.
The hotel's confirmation email said, "**Please note that** check-in is not available before 3 p.m."

drill.sentence: Your appointment is confirmed for May 3. {{Please note that}} you must arrive fifteen minutes early to fill out forms.
drill.hint: formal way to draw attention to a detail (not *… be aware* or *Keep in mind*)

entries.related: *please be aware that* — more formal, often for risks; *keep in mind that* — friendlier; *just a heads-up* — informal advance warning.

entries.term: let me know what you think
entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: Asks someone for their opinion or feedback on something you have sent or suggested.
entries.usage: Very common at the end of emails with a draft, plan or idea: *I've attached the draft; let me know what you think*. It is friendly and open, and it works with colleagues, clients and friends. For a more formal tone, use *I'd appreciate your feedback* or *I'd welcome your comments*.
examples: I've attached two versions of the logo; **let me know what you think** before Friday.
My sister sent me a photo of her wedding dress with the message "**Let me know what you think**!"
The new clinic hours start in May, so please **let us know what you think** in the patient survey.

drill.sentence: I've drafted a reply to the client. Could you read it and {{let me know what you think}}?
drill.hint: give me your opinion of it (not *tell me …*)

entries.related: *any thoughts?* — casual and short; *I'd appreciate your feedback* — more formal; *happy to hear any suggestions* — invites changes.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: Do something without waiting any longer, either because you have permission or because you have decided to act.
entries.usage: Very common in American speech and email. *I've gone ahead and…* tells someone you've already acted, which saves an extra round of email, and *Feel free to go ahead and…* gives permission. It adds little meaning, so service staff often use it as a filler (*Let me go ahead and…*), and in formal writing you can usually leave it out.
entries.pattern: go ahead and + verb; I've gone ahead and + past participle
examples: Nobody replied about the room, so I **went ahead and** booked it for Thursday.
If the printer jams again, just **go ahead and** call IT; don't wait for me.
"Let me **go ahead and** pull up your account," the agent said on the phone.

drill.sentence: Since everyone agreed on the menu, I've {{gone ahead and}} ordered the food for Friday.
drill.hint: acted without waiting for more discussion — informal US (not *already*)

entries.related: *feel free to* — gives permission; *take the liberty of* — formal, act without asking; *jump the gun* — act too early.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To send someone a copy of an email by adding their address to the *cc* line, so that they are informed but are not the main reader.
entries.usage: Common in work email: *I've cc'd Anna on this* or *Please cc me on your reply*. People cc a manager or a colleague who needs to know, but cc'ing someone's boss on a complaint can feel like pressure. The past form is usually written *cc'd* (also *cc'ed*), and *bcc* hides the address from the other readers.
entries.pattern: cc someone (on an email / a reply)
examples: I've **cc'd** Dr. Ahmed, who manages the sequencing facility, so she can answer your question directly.
Please **cc** me on any emails to the landlord so I know what's going on.
The teacher **cc'd** the principal on her reply, which made the parent even angrier.

drill.sentence: I'll {{cc}} our accountant on my reply so she can see the numbers too.
drill.hint: add her to the email as a second reader — two-letter verb (not *copy*)

entries.related: *copy someone on* — same meaning, a bit more neutral (British also *copy someone in*); *loop someone in* — informal, add someone to a conversation; *bcc* — send a hidden copy.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: Asks someone to tell you when they are free, so you can schedule a meeting or call.
entries.usage: Common in scheduling emails: *Please let me know your availability for a 30-minute call next week*. It is neutral and polite but a little stiff; *When are you free?* or *What times work for you?* sounds friendlier. Give a time frame so the answer is useful, or offer two or three slots yourself.
entries.pattern: (Please) let me know your availability (for + meeting) (next week)
examples: We'd like to invite you for an interview. Please **let me know your availability** next week.
My cousin is planning a reunion and asked us all to **let her know our availability** for July.
The contractor wrote, "Please **let me know your availability** so we can schedule the inspection."

drill.sentence: I'd like to set up a short call to discuss the contract. Please {{let me know your availability}} this week.
drill.hint: tell me when you're free — five words (not *send me …* or *… what times work*)

entries.related: *what times work for you?* — friendlier; *when are you free?* — casual; *here's my availability* — offers your own free times.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To contact someone by email, phone or message.
entries.usage: Very common in emails, on websites and in speech: *Feel free to get in touch if you have questions*. It is neutral and friendly, fine for both strangers and friends. *I'll be in touch* promises future contact, *keep in touch* means stay in contact over time, and *reach out* is a more corporate American alternative.
entries.pattern: get in touch (with someone) (about something)
examples: If you're interested in joining the study, please **get in touch** with Dr. Park's office.
I finally **got in touch with** my old college roommate after ten years.
Police have asked anyone who saw the accident to **get in touch**.

drill.sentence: I lost his number, but I'll try to {{get in touch with}} him through his sister.
drill.hint: make contact — fixed phrase (not *reach out to* or *contact*)

entries.related: *contact* — more formal; *reach out (to)* — common in American business email; *keep in touch* — stay in contact over time.

entries.term: put someone in touch with someone
entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To introduce two people, usually by giving one the other's contact details, so that they can talk directly.
entries.usage: Common in work emails and networking: *Could you put me in touch with someone in HR?* It is neutral and polite, and it is a normal favor to ask a colleague or advisor. In email the introduction itself is often called *an intro*, and Americans also say *connect someone with someone*.
entries.pattern: put A in touch with B
examples: My advisor **put me in touch with** a former student who now works at NASA.
Could you **put me in touch with** a good plumber? Ours retired last year.
The hospital social worker **put** my parents **in touch with** a support group.

drill.sentence: You both work on sleep research, so I'd be happy to {{put you in touch with}} her if you'd like to talk.
drill.hint: give you her contact details so you two can talk (not *connect you with* or *introduce you to*)

entries.related: *connect someone with someone* — same, a little more American; *introduce* — more formal; *a warm intro* — an introduction from someone both people know.

entries.term: thank you for taking the time to …
entries.spoken_term: thank you for taking the time to
entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: Thanks someone for the time and effort they spent doing something for you, such as meeting, reading or replying.
entries.usage: Common in follow-up emails after interviews, meetings and favors: *Thank you for taking the time to meet with me yesterday*. It is polite and slightly formal, and it shows you know the person is busy. It is followed by a verb; without one, say *Thank you for your time*.
entries.pattern: Thank you for taking the time to + verb
examples: **Thank you for taking the time to** meet with me yesterday; I really enjoyed learning about the team.
**Thank you for taking the time to** fill out our customer survey.
I wanted to **thank** our neighbor **for taking the time to** teach my son to ride a bike.

drill.sentence: Dear Dr. Osei, {{thank you for taking the time to}} read my proposal and send such detailed comments.
drill.hint: polite gratitude for the effort someone spent — seven words (not *thanks …*)

entries.related: *thank you for your time* — shorter, with no verb after it; *I appreciate you taking the time to* — a little warmer; *thanks for making time* — informal.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Starting from a particular date or time; with a past date or *today*, it can also mean at that point in time.
entries.usage: Common in announcements and work email: *As of Monday, all visitors must sign in at the front desk*. With a past or present time, it often reports a current state: *As of this morning, we've received 40 applications*. It is neutral and slightly formal; in speech, *starting Monday* is more common.
entries.pattern: As of + date / time / now
examples: **As of** next Monday, all lab visitors must wear closed-toe shoes.
**As of** this morning, the flight was still listed as on time.
**As of** January, the gym's monthly fee goes up to fifty dollars.

drill.sentence: {{As of}} July 1, the clinic will no longer accept walk-in patients.
drill.hint: the change takes effect on that date — two short words (not *Starting*, *Beginning*, *Effective* or *From*)

entries.related: *starting* — more common in speech; *effective* — formal, for rules and policies; *as from* — mainly British.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: An informal opening for a short email that has one simple purpose.
entries.usage: Common with colleagues, friends and people you know: *Just a quick note to say thanks for yesterday*. It tells the reader the message is short and needs little effort. It is followed by *to* + verb (*say*, *let you know*, *remind you*); for formal emails, use *I'm writing to…* instead.
entries.pattern: Just a quick note to + verb
examples: Hi Kim, **just a quick note to** say the samples arrived safely this morning.
**Just a quick note to** remind everyone that the potluck is this Saturday at six.
Hi Mrs. Lopez, **just a quick note to** let you know that Mia loved the class trip.

drill.sentence: {{Just a quick note to}} say thanks for covering my shift on Saturday. I owe you one!
drill.hint: casual opener for a short message — five words (not *I'm writing to* or *… email to*)

entries.related: *I'm writing to* — neutral to formal; *just a heads-up* — informal warning; *just checking in* — a light request for an update.

entries.term: please don't hesitate to contact me
entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: A formal closing line telling the reader that they are welcome to contact you if they need anything.
entries.usage: Standard near the end of formal or customer-facing emails: *If you have any questions, please don't hesitate to contact me*. It is polite but stiff, and many people find it a cliché. With colleagues, *Let me know if you have any questions* or *Feel free to reach out* sounds more natural.
entries.pattern: If …, please don't hesitate to contact me
examples: If you need any more information about the rental, **please don't hesitate to contact me**.
Our office manager ends every email with "**Please don't hesitate to contact me**," even though she sits ten feet away from us.
If your son has any trouble with the new medication, **please don't hesitate to contact me**.

drill.sentence: If you have any questions about your new benefits, {{please don't hesitate to contact me}} by phone or email.
drill.hint: formal stock line: feel welcome to get in touch (not *feel free to …* or *reach out*)

entries.related: *feel free to reach out* — friendlier, American; *let me know if you have any questions* — neutral; *I'm happy to help* — warm.

entries.label: formal greeting
entries.meaning: A formal greeting for a letter or email when you do not know the reader's name or who will read it.
entries.usage: Used for documents that any reader might receive, such as employment confirmations, reference letters and complaints to an office. In ordinary email it sounds cold and old-fashioned, so first try to find a name or use a role: *Dear Hiring Manager*, *Dear Admissions Committee*.
examples: **To Whom It May Concern**: This letter confirms that Ms. Diaz worked at our clinic from 2019 to 2024.
My cover letter began with "**To Whom It May Concern**," and my career coach told me to find a real name.
Our office still gets letters addressed "**To Whom It May Concern**," usually from companies selling something.

drill.sentence: I didn't know who reads complaints at the city office, so I started my letter with {{To Whom It May Concern}}.
drill.hint: formal greeting for an unknown reader (not *Dear Sir or Madam*)

entries.related: *Dear Sir or Madam* — similar, more British; *Dear Hiring Manager* — a role, warmer and more modern; *Hello* — for general inboxes in casual contexts.

entries.label: email greeting
entries.meaning: A standard friendly greeting for an email to a group of people.
entries.usage: The usual way to open a group email in American workplaces, labs and schools, followed by a comma. *Hi everyone* is just as common and a little warmer, while *Dear all* sounds stiff to many Americans. *Hi guys* is common among friends but can feel too casual for a mixed or senior group.
examples: **Hi all**, just a reminder that the lab meeting moves to Room 204 this week.
My manager starts every team email with "**Hi all**," even when there are only two of us.
**Hi all**, thanks for coming to the parents' meeting last night; the notes are attached.

drill.sentence: {{Hi all}}, the elevator in Building C will be out of service until Thursday, so please use the stairs.
drill.hint: standard friendly greeting for a group email, two words (not *Dear all*, *Hey all* or *Hi everyone*)

entries.related: *Hi everyone* — same, slightly warmer; *Hello all* — a little more formal; *Dear all* — formal, common in British and international email.

entries.label: letter sign-off
entries.meaning: A formal sign-off used at the end of letters, cover letters and very formal emails, just before your name.
entries.usage: Standard in American cover letters, recommendation letters and official correspondence. In everyday work email it sounds stiff, so most people use *Best* or *Best regards* instead. British English puts *Yours sincerely* in the same place, while Americans usually write just *Sincerely* or *Sincerely yours*.
examples: I would welcome the chance to discuss the position further. **Sincerely**, Maya Brooks
My cover letter ended with "**Sincerely**," but my emails to the team just say "Thanks."
The letter from the insurance company was signed "**Sincerely**, Claims Department."

drill.sentence: Thank you again for your time, and I hope to speak with you soon about the teaching position. {{Sincerely}}, James Ortiz
drill.hint: formal one-word sign-off for a cover letter (not *Regards*, *Respectfully* or *Best*)

entries.related: *Yours sincerely* — the British form; *Best regards* — less formal, for email; *Respectfully* — very formal, for officials.

entries.label: email sign-off
entries.meaning: A polite, slightly warm sign-off for work emails, just before your name.
entries.usage: Common in business email in both the US and the UK, especially to clients and people you don't know well. It is a little warmer than *Regards* alone, which can sound cold, and about as formal as *Best regards*. With colleagues you write to every day, *Thanks* or *Best* is more relaxed.
examples: Thanks again for sending the contract so quickly. **Kind regards**, Olivia Grant
Her emails to clients always end with "**Kind regards**," never just "Thanks."
The preschool's newsletter closed with "**Kind regards** from all of us at Little Oaks."

drill.sentence: We'll have the revised quote to you by Friday. {{Kind regards}}, Sam Lee, Sales Team
drill.hint: polite, slightly warm two-word sign-off (not *Best …* or *Warm …*)

entries.related: *Best regards* — very close, slightly more neutral; *Regards* — short, can sound cold; *Warm regards* — friendlier, for people you know.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Formal: concerning, or about, a particular subject.
entries.usage: Used in formal emails, letters and reports, often at the start of a sentence to introduce a topic: *With regard to your request, …*. The correct form is singular *regard*; *with regards to* is common but widely seen as an error. In normal email, *about* or *regarding* is usually simpler.
entries.pattern: with regard to + noun
examples: **With regard to** your question about vacation days, unused days carry over to next year.
The school has not yet made a decision **with regard to** next year's start time.
The hospital updated its rules **with regard to** visitors in the ICU.

drill.sentence: {{With regard to}} your request for an extension, I'm happy to give you one more week.
drill.hint: formal: on the subject of — three words starting with *With* (not *… respect to*)

mistake.wrong: With regards to your question, the deadline is Friday.
mistake.right: With regard to your question, the deadline is Friday.
mistake.why: In this phrase *regard* is singular; *regards* belongs in sign-offs like *Best regards*.

entries.related: *regarding* — one word, very common in email; *with respect to* — formal, also in academic writing; *as for* — introduces a new topic, more conversational.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: In the way that you asked for; used when you send or do something that someone requested.
entries.usage: Common at the start of work emails that deliver something: *As requested, I've attached the signed forms*. It is efficient and polite but a little formal and impersonal. With a friendly reader, *Here's the … you asked for* sounds warmer.
examples: **As requested**, I've attached the signed consent form and a copy of my insurance card.
**As requested**, the meeting has been moved to Room 3B on the third floor.
The hotel left two extra pillows and a fan in our room, **as requested**.

drill.sentence: {{As requested}}, here are the photos of the damage to the car for your insurance claim.
drill.hint: because you asked for them — two words, formal (not *As promised* or *As discussed*)

mistake.wrong: As requested, please find enclosed the documents.
mistake.right: As requested, I've attached the documents.
mistake.why: *Enclosed* is for paper letters; in an email, files are *attached*.

entries.related: *as promised* — you said you would do it; *as discussed* — refers to an earlier conversation; *per your request* — more formal and stiff.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: As a reply to something, such as an email, question or ad.
entries.usage: Used in formal emails and letters, often as the opening: *In response to your email of May 3, …*. It is clear but stiff; in normal work email, *Thanks for your email* sounds friendlier. It also describes actions taken because of something: *The school changed its policy in response to complaints*.
entries.pattern: in response to + email / question / request / complaints
examples: **In response to** your email of March 12, I can confirm that your refund has been processed.
The city added more buses **in response to** complaints about overcrowding.
I'm writing **in response to** your ad for a part-time lab technician.

drill.sentence: {{In response to}} your question about the dress code, business casual is fine for the interview.
drill.hint: formal: as a reply to — three words (not *in reply to*, *in answer to* or *with regard to*)

entries.related: *in reply to* — very close, mainly for messages; *following up on* — continues an earlier exchange; *regarding* — about, not necessarily a reply.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: Politely asks someone to say that a fact, time or arrangement is correct or agreed.
entries.usage: Very common in work email to avoid misunderstandings: *Could you confirm that the meeting is still on for Tuesday?* It is followed by a noun or a *that* / *whether* clause, never directly by a person. *Can you confirm* is slightly more casual, and *Could you please confirm* slightly more formal.
entries.pattern: Could you confirm + noun / that … / whether …?
examples: **Could you confirm** that the venue can seat sixty people for the dinner?
**Could you confirm** whether my son's medical form arrived before the camp deadline?
Before I book the flights, **could you confirm** the dates of the workshop?

drill.sentence: We have two addresses on file for your company. {{Could you confirm}} which one the invoice should go to?
drill.hint: politely ask them to say which is correct (not *verify*, *check* or *tell me*)

mistake.wrong: Could you confirm me the date of the exam?
mistake.right: Could you confirm the date of the exam for me?
mistake.why: Unlike *give me* or *send me*, *confirm* cannot be followed directly by a person; say *confirm something (for someone)*.

entries.related: *could you verify* — check that something is correct, more technical; *just to confirm* — you state the fact and ask for a yes; *can you double-check* — informal.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: Given so that you can look at or check it if you need to, without any action being required.
entries.usage: Common in work email when you attach or paste background material: *I've attached last year's report for your reference*. It is neutral to slightly formal and signals that the reader does not have to do anything with it. *FYI* is the casual version; *for your review* means you do want comments or approval.
examples: I've attached last year's budget **for your reference**; the new numbers are in the second tab.
**For your reference**, the parking garage closes at 10 p.m. on weekdays.
Here's the full season schedule **for your reference**; away games are marked in red.

drill.sentence: No need to do anything with this; I'm just sending the floor plan {{for your reference}}.
drill.hint: to look at if needed, no action required (not *… information*, *… records* or *… review*)

entries.related: *FYI* — for your information, casual; *for your records* — for you to keep; *for your review* — please check and comment.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: Sent so that the reader can check something and give comments or approval.
entries.usage: Common in work email when you send a draft, contract or plan to someone who must look at it: *Attached is the draft for your review*. Unlike *for your reference*, it asks for action, so add a deadline if you need one. *For your approval* is stronger: you need a yes.
examples: Attached is the revised grant budget **for your review**; please send any comments by Friday.
I've shared the draft lease **for your review** before we both sign it.
The school's email read: "Your child's report card is attached **for your review**."

drill.sentence: I've attached the final version of the contract {{for your review}}. Please let me know if anything needs to change.
drill.hint: so you can check it and comment (not *… reference*, *… approval* or *… consideration*)

entries.related: *for your reference* — no action needed; *for your approval* — you need a decision; *for your signature* — the reader must sign.

entries.label: formal phrase
entries.meaning: A formal apology for trouble caused to customers or users, for example by a delay, closure or change.
entries.usage: Standard in notices, service emails and announcements from companies and institutions. It is polite but impersonal, and some readers find it empty because it does not name a specific problem. In a personal email, *Sorry for the trouble* or a specific apology sounds more sincere.
entries.pattern: We apologize for any inconvenience (this may cause)
examples: The east entrance will be closed for repairs until Friday. **We apologize for any inconvenience**.
The airline's text said only that the flight was canceled and that it **apologized for any inconvenience**.
**We apologize for any inconvenience** this may cause; the system should be back by noon.

drill.sentence: Our online store will be down for maintenance on Sunday morning. {{We apologize for any inconvenience}}.
drill.hint: formal, impersonal apology for whatever trouble this causes (not *We regret …* or *Sorry for …*)

entries.related: *we regret any inconvenience* — even more formal; *sorry for the trouble* — personal and simple; *thank you for your patience* — thanks people for waiting.

entries.label: formal phrase
entries.meaning: Formal thanks for accepting a problem, delay or refusal patiently.
entries.usage: Common at the end of notices and service emails, usually right after bad news such as a closure, a delay or a refusal. It thanks the reader in advance, so it can feel pushy if they have not accepted anything yet. *Thank you for your patience* is used for waiting and delays.
examples: Because of staff illness, today's yoga class is canceled. **Thank you for your understanding**.
My landlord ended his email about the rent increase with "**Thank you for your understanding**," which annoyed me.
We're unable to offer refunds once the tour has started, and we **thank you for your understanding**.

drill.sentence: Because of the storm, all deliveries will be one day late this week. {{Thank you for your understanding}}.
drill.hint: formal thanks for accepting the problem calmly (not *… patience*)

entries.related: *thank you for your patience* — for waiting; *we apologize for any inconvenience* — a formal apology, often used with it; *thanks for bearing with us* — warmer.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To send an email or message you received on to another person.
entries.usage: Common in work email: *I'll forward you the invitation* or *Could you forward this to the team?* Both *forward someone something* and *forward something to someone* are correct. Before forwarding, check the thread below for anything private, and add a line explaining why you're sending it.
entries.pattern: forward something (to someone) / forward someone something
examples: I'll **forward** you the email from the dean so you can see exactly what she asked for.
Could you **forward** this to anyone in your building who might want a free couch?
My mom **forwards** me every article about healthy eating that she finds.

drill.sentence: I'm not the right person for this, but I'll {{forward}} your email to our billing department.
drill.hint: pass it on to another person by email — one verb (not *send*)

entries.related: *send on* — same idea, more general; *loop someone in* — add them to the thread instead; *Fwd:* — the label added to a forwarded email's subject line.

entries.term: thank you for bringing this to my attention
entries.label: formal phrase
entries.meaning: A formal way to thank someone for telling you about a problem or mistake.
entries.usage: Common in customer service, management and official replies to complaints. It is polite and shows that you take the problem seriously, but it should be followed by what you will do about it. With colleagues, *Thanks for flagging this* or *Thanks for letting me know* is more natural.
examples: **Thank you for bringing this to my attention**; I've asked IT to fix the error today.
When I reported the broken railing, the building manager said, "**Thank you for bringing this to my attention**."
I'm sorry your grade was entered incorrectly, and **thank you for bringing this to my attention**.

drill.sentence: Dear Ms. Grant, {{thank you for bringing this to my attention}}. I've corrected the charge on your account.
drill.hint: formal thanks for telling me about the problem (not *for letting me know*)

entries.related: *thanks for flagging this* — informal, common at work; *thanks for letting me know* — neutral; *thanks for the heads-up* — informal, for a warning.

entries.label: adverbial phrase
entries.meaning: During the time until something expected happens, or while waiting for it.
entries.usage: Very common in emails when you can't do something yet and offer a temporary step: *The part arrives next week; in the meantime, please use the other printer*. It is neutral and fits all registers. *Meanwhile* is close but is more often used for two things happening at the same time, especially in stories and news.
examples: The new laptops arrive next week; **in the meantime**, you can borrow one from IT.
My passport won't be ready for six weeks, so **in the meantime** I can't book any trips abroad.
The specialist can't see you until March, but **in the meantime** try to rest your knee.

drill.sentence: The repair person can't come until Tuesday. {{In the meantime}}, please don't use the dishwasher.
drill.hint: during the wait before that happens — three words (not *Meanwhile* or *Until …*)

entries.related: *meanwhile* — at the same time, often in stories; *for now* — at the moment, until things change; *until then* — up to that time.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Comments written directly inside a text, such as answers inserted into a quoted email or notes placed at specific points in a document or code.
entries.usage: Common in work email and document or code review: *I've added my answers inline, in red*. It saves the reader from matching answers to questions. In email, say how they are marked (*see my comments inline below, in blue*), since color may not show on every device.
examples: I've added **inline comments** in blue below, so you can see my answer to each question.
The editor's **inline comments** on my article were short but very useful.
Our team lead leaves **inline comments** on every pull request, right next to the lines she wants changed.

drill.sentence: Please don't send me a list of changes; just leave {{inline comments}} in the shared draft wherever something is unclear.
drill.hint: two-word term for notes placed at the exact spot in the text (not *margin …*)

entries.related: *comments in the margin* — notes beside the text in a document; *track changes* — edits shown in the text; *reply inline* — answer inside the quoted message.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: An editing mode, for example in Microsoft Word, that records and shows every change made to a document so that others can accept or reject it.
entries.usage: Common when people edit contracts, papers and reports together: *I've made my edits in track changes*. You *turn on* or *use* track changes, and the other person *accepts* or *rejects* each change. In Google Docs, the similar feature is *Suggesting* mode.
entries.pattern: edit with / in track changes; turn on track changes
examples: Please make your edits in **track changes** so I can see exactly what you changed.
Our lawyer sent back the lease with **track changes**, and nearly every page was covered in red.
My teacher marks our essays using **track changes**, so we can learn from each correction.

drill.sentence: Before you edit the contract, turn on {{track changes}} so the client can see every word we change.
drill.hint: Word's editing mode that shows each edit (not *Suggesting mode*)

entries.related: *Suggesting mode* — the Google Docs version; *a redline* — a marked-up version of a contract, mainly in law; *a clean copy* — a version with all changes accepted.

entries.spoken_term: we regret to inform you that
entries.label: formal phrase
entries.meaning: A formal, impersonal opening for bad news, such as a rejection or a cancellation.
entries.usage: Typical of official letters from universities, journals, employers and companies: *We regret to inform you that your paper was not accepted*. It is formal and distant, so in a personal message *I'm sorry to tell you that…* or *Unfortunately, …* is kinder. Note the infinitive: *regret to inform* is about news you are giving now, while *regret informing* would mean you are sorry you did it.
entries.pattern: We regret to inform you (that) + bad news
examples: The museum **regrets to inform** visitors **that** the west wing is closed until further notice.
**We regret to inform you that** your paper was not accepted for this year's workshop.
The email opened with "**We regret to inform you**," so I didn't need to read the rest.

drill.sentence: Dear Mr. Okafor, {{we regret to inform you}} that the position you applied for has already been filled.
drill.hint: formal opening for bad news (not *we are sorry to …*)

entries.related: *unfortunately* — simpler and warmer; *I'm sorry to tell you that* — personal; *we are pleased to inform you* — the formal opening for good news.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To formally ask for more time before a deadline, for example for an assignment, application or payment.
entries.usage: Common in emails to professors, editors, funders and offices: *I'm writing to request an extension on the report*. It is neutral to formal; *ask for an extension* is more everyday. A good request gives a short reason and proposes a new date, and the task follows *on* or *for* (*an extension on the essay*).
entries.pattern: request an extension (on / for + task) (until + date)
examples: My father was in the hospital last week, so I'd like to **request an extension** on the final essay.
The company **requested an extension** on its tax filing after a fire destroyed its records.
Our team plans to **request an extension** until June, since the equipment arrived three months late.

drill.sentence: My laptop died two days before the deadline, so I emailed my professor to {{request an extension}} on the paper.
drill.hint: formally ask for more time — verb + noun (not *ask for …*)

entries.related: *ask for an extension* — everyday; *grant an extension* — what the professor or office does; *a no-cost extension* — more time on a grant without extra money.

entries.term: thank you for your time and consideration
entries.label: formal phrase
entries.meaning: A formal closing line that thanks the reader for reading and thinking about your application or request.
entries.usage: Standard in cover letters, applications and formal requests, just before the sign-off. It is polite and expected in these settings, but it sounds too formal for everyday work email. A shorter version is *Thank you for your consideration*.
examples: I've attached my CV and two writing samples. **Thank you for your time and consideration**.
My grant proposal ended with "**Thank you for your time and consideration**," just like every cover letter I've written.
**Thank you for your time and consideration**, and I hope to hear from you about the apartment soon.

drill.sentence: I would be glad to discuss my experience in an interview. {{Thank you for your time and consideration}}.
drill.hint: formal closing: gratitude for reading and weighing my application (not *for reading*)

entries.related: *thank you for your consideration* — shorter, same use; *thank you for your time* — after a meeting or reply; *I look forward to hearing from you* — often comes just before it.

entries.label: abbreviation
entries.meaning: Short for *as soon as possible*: right away, or very soon.
entries.usage: Common in work email and chat, and in speech it is said either as letters, *A-S-A-P*, or as a word, *AY-sap*. In email it can sound demanding or stressed, especially to a senior person or a client, so a specific deadline (*by 3 p.m. today*) is often clearer and more polite. Use it mainly with people you know well.
examples: The printer is out of toner and the board meets at two, so please order more **ASAP**.
Call me back **ASAP**; the babysitter just canceled for tonight.
The landlord promised to fix the heat **ASAP**, but it's been a week.

drill.sentence: The patient's blood test results look odd, so I need the lab to rerun them {{ASAP}}.
drill.hint: abbreviation: right away, as quickly as you can (not *now*)

entries.related: *at your earliest convenience* — formal, but often means soon; *EOD* — by the end of the workday; *when you get a chance* — no rush.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A short letter sent with a job application or a paper submission that introduces you or your work and explains why it is a good fit.
entries.usage: Standard in American job applications and in academic publishing: you send *a cover letter* with your résumé, or with a manuscript to a journal editor. It should be addressed to a person or role if possible and written for that specific job or journal. British English often says *covering letter*.
examples: Most journals ask for **a cover letter** explaining why the paper fits their readers.
I rewrote **my cover letter** for each job instead of sending the same one to fifty companies.
The nursing program wanted a résumé, two references and **a cover letter** by March 1.

drill.sentence: Along with your résumé, please include {{a cover letter}} explaining why you want to work at our clinic.
drill.hint: the one-page introduction that goes with an application (not *a personal statement*)

entries.related: *a covering letter* — British; *a personal statement* — a longer essay for university admissions; *a statement of purpose* — for graduate school applications.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A letter in which a professor, employer or supervisor supports a candidate for a job, program or award.
entries.usage: Standard in American academic and job applications: *Could you write me a letter of recommendation?* It is also called *a recommendation letter*, *a reference letter* or, informally, *a rec letter*. In British English, *a reference* is the more common word.
examples: I need three **letters of recommendation** for my PhD applications, and one professor hasn't replied yet.
My old soccer coach wrote **a letter of recommendation** that helped me get into college.
The new nurse arrived with **a letter of recommendation** from the head of her last hospital.

drill.sentence: Professor Kim, would you be willing to write {{a letter of recommendation}} for my application to the summer program?
drill.hint: a written statement supporting my application, four words (not *a reference*)

entries.related: *a reference* — British, or a person you name to be contacted; *a recommender* — the person who writes it; *a rec letter* — informal, among students.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: An out-of-office phrase meaning that you will rarely read your email while you are away.
entries.usage: Standard in automatic out-of-office replies: *I'm traveling with limited access to email until June 3*. It politely tells people not to expect a quick answer without promising no reply at all. It is usually followed by the date you return and someone to contact for urgent matters.
entries.pattern: I will have / I'm traveling with limited access to email (until + date)
examples: I'll be at my sister's wedding in Mexico and **will have limited access to email** until Monday.
Thank you for your message. I'm on vacation **with limited access to email** until July 10.
The researchers **had limited access to email** during their three weeks at the Arctic station.

drill.sentence: I'm away for a family emergency and {{will have limited access to email}} until next Wednesday.
drill.hint: rarely be able to read messages — out-of-office formula (not *be offline*)

entries.related: *out of office* (*OOO*) — away from work; *an auto-reply* — the automatic message; *for urgent matters, please contact* — the usual next line.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To be absent from work or school because you are ill.
entries.usage: Very common in American workplaces and schools, in speech and email: *Maria is out sick today*. It is neutral and polite and does not give details of the illness. The British equivalent is *off sick*, and *call in sick* means telling your workplace that you won't come.
entries.pattern: be out sick (today / with + illness)
examples: Dr. Gomez **is out sick** today, so all her appointments have been moved to Thursday.
Half my son's class **was out sick** with the flu last week.
Sorry for the slow reply; I **was out sick** most of last week.

drill.sentence: Jen won't be at the meeting; she's {{out sick}} with a bad cold.
drill.hint: absent from work because she's ill — US (not *home …* or British *off …*)

entries.related: *call in sick* — phone to say you won't come; *off sick* — British; *a sick day* — a day off because of illness.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The line at the top of an email that states its topic and appears in the reader's inbox before the email is opened.
entries.usage: Important in work email, because many people decide from it whether to open a message, so make it short and specific: *Room change for Friday's workshop*. You put information *in the subject line*. Words like *Urgent* or *Action needed* make a message sound pressing, so use them only when it really is.
examples: Please put your student ID in **the subject line** so I can find your email quickly.
**The subject line** said "You've won a cruise," so I deleted it without opening it.
My boss replied to an old thread, so **the subject line** still said "Holiday party."

drill.sentence: Your email got lost because {{the subject line}} just said "Hi," so nobody knew what it was about.
drill.hint: the short heading that shows in the inbox (not *the title*)

entries.related: *the body* — the main text of an email; *the preview text* — the first words shown in the inbox; *Re:* and *Fwd:* — labels for replies and forwards.

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: A polite reply when someone reminds you about a task, deadline or appointment.
entries.usage: Common in email and in person, especially when you forgot or are late: *Thank you for the reminder; I'll send it today*. It accepts the reminder politely without sounding defensive, and it is best to add when you'll act. *Thanks for the reminder* is more casual.
examples: **Thank you for the reminder**; I'll have the signed form to you by noon.
**Thanks for the reminder** about Dad's birthday. I'd completely forgotten!
When the dentist's office called, I said, "**Thank you for the reminder**," and wrote it on the calendar.

drill.sentence: Hi Dr. Chen, {{thank you for the reminder}}. I'll submit my timesheet before the end of the day.
drill.hint: polite reply to someone who nudged you about a task (not *thanks for letting me know*)

entries.related: *thanks for the heads-up* — for a warning about something coming; *a gentle reminder* — a polite nudge from the other side; *it slipped my mind* — I forgot.

entries.label: fixed phrase
entries.meaning: At or before a stated time or date; this is the final deadline.
entries.usage: Common in formal emails, instructions and official notices: *Applications must be received no later than May 1*. It is firm and clear and shows that the deadline is strict. In friendly emails, *by May 1* says the same thing more softly.
entries.pattern: no later than + time / date
examples: Please submit your expense reports **no later than** the fifth of each month.
Guests must check out of their rooms **no later than** 11 a.m.
We need to leave the house **no later than** six if we want to make the flight.

drill.sentence: Final grades must be entered {{no later than}} noon on Friday, December 18.
drill.hint: at or before this deadline — formal, three words (not *by* or *before*)

entries.related: *by* — plainer, same meaning; *before* — strictly earlier than the time; *at the latest* — comes after the time (*by Friday at the latest*).

entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: A polite way to ask for a little of someone's time, suggesting that the request is small and not urgent.
entries.usage: Common in emails and in person, especially with busy or senior people: *If you have a moment, could you look over my slides?* It softens a request and gives the other person an easy way to say no. *When you get a chance* is similar and suggests even less urgency.
examples: **If you have a moment** today, could you look over my slides for tomorrow's talk?
Excuse me, **if you have a moment**, could you help me find the train to the airport?
Our neighbor knocked and said, "**If you have a moment**, I'd love to show you our new garden."

drill.sentence: Hi Professor Diaz, {{if you have a moment}} this week, I'd love to ask you a few questions about the course.
drill.hint: if you can spare a little — polite (not *… minute*, *… chance* or *… time*)

entries.related: *when you get a chance* — even less urgent; *do you have a minute?* — spoken, asks to talk now; *no rush* — added to show it isn't urgent.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To allow someone to open, view or edit a file, folder or system, or to enter a place.
entries.usage: Common in work email and with shared tools: *Could you give me access to the shared drive?* *Access* here is uncountable, so do not say *an access* or *accesses*. With documents, people also say *share the file with someone*, and *grant access* is more formal.
entries.pattern: give someone access to + file / folder / system; request / grant access
examples: IT will **give** you **access to** the shared drive on your first day.
The hotel **gave** us **access to** the pool even after we checked out.
New nurses aren't **given access to** the medication cabinet until they finish training.

drill.sentence: I can't open the budget spreadsheet; it says I need permission. Could you {{give me access}} to it?
drill.hint: allow me to open it — everyday verb (not *grant me …* or *share it with me*)

mistake.wrong: Could you give me an access to the folder?
mistake.right: Could you give me access to the folder?
mistake.why: *Access* is uncountable in this sense, so it takes no *an*.

entries.related: *grant access* — formal; *share something with someone* — for files and documents; *request access* — ask for it, often with a button in the app.

entries.term: I would be grateful if you could …
entries.spoken_term: I would be grateful if you could
entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: A formal, polite way to ask someone to do something, common in first emails to people you don't know.
entries.usage: Used in formal emails and letters, for example to professors, offices or officials: *I would be grateful if you could send me the form*. It is very polite but can sound stiff in American email, where *Could you please…?* or *I'd appreciate it if you could…* is more common. The usual form pairs *would* with *could*.
entries.pattern: I would be grateful if you could + verb
examples: **I would be grateful if you could** send me a copy of the syllabus before the semester starts.
We **would be grateful if you could** keep the noise down after 10 p.m. on weeknights.
In her email to the consulate, she wrote, "**I would be grateful if you could** confirm my appointment."

drill.sentence: Dear Dr. Nakamura, {{I would be grateful if you could}} tell me whether your lab is accepting new students this year.
drill.hint: formal, very polite request — seven words (not *I'd appreciate it …*)

entries.related: *I'd appreciate it if you could* — a little less formal; *could you please* — direct and polite; *would you mind* + *-ing* — polite, a little softer.

entries.label: email greeting
entries.meaning: The standard formal greeting for an email to a professor: the title plus the professor's last name.
entries.usage: Use it for a first email or when you don't know the professor well, especially as a student or applicant. Never combine the title with the first name; if you're not sure the person is a professor, *Dear Dr.* + last name is safe for anyone with a doctorate. Once the professor signs with a first name, you can usually switch to it.
entries.pattern: Dear Professor + last name,
examples: **Dear Professor Hughes**, I'm a junior in your Tuesday seminar, and I have a question about the final project.
My daughter's first email to her advisor began "**Dear Professor Lin**," and he replied, "Call me David."
I wasn't sure whether to write **Dear Professor Shah** or Dear Dr. Shah, so I checked the department website.

drill.sentence: {{Dear Professor}} Martinez, I'm writing to ask whether there are still open spots in your seminar.
drill.hint: formal greeting + academic title (not *Hi …* or *… Dr.*)

mistake.why: A title such as *Professor*, *Dr.* or *Mr.* goes with the last name, never the first name (so not *Dear Mr. John* either).

entries.related: *Dear Dr.* + last name — also safe; *Hi Professor* + last name — common among American students once they know the professor; *Dear Sir* — avoid, it sounds dated.

entries.term: thank you for your prompt reply
entries.label: email phrase
entries.meaning: A formal way to thank someone who answered your message quickly.
entries.usage: Common at the start of a reply in formal or semi-formal emails, for example with offices, clients and professors. *Prompt* means quick and on time and sounds a little formal; *Thanks for the quick reply* is more relaxed. Avoid *Thank you in advance for your prompt reply*, which reads as pressure.
examples: **Thank you for your prompt reply**; the dates you suggested work perfectly for us.
Dear Mr. Evans, **thank you for your prompt reply** about the water damage in the basement.
The permit office answered my question within an hour, so my reply began, "**Thank you for your prompt reply**."

drill.sentence: Dear Ms. Ito, {{thank you for your prompt reply}}. I've filled out the form and attached it here.
drill.hint: formal thanks for answering quickly (not *… quick …* or *… fast …*)

entries.related: *thanks for the quick reply* — more relaxed; *thanks for getting back to me* — neutral, says nothing about speed; *apologies for the delay* — when you are the slow one.
